newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia pushes for Asia trade amid race debate.
newsitem.headline: Australia pushes for Asia trade amid race debate.

text.p: Australia on Monday launched a promotional push for more trade with Asia in the lead-up to the Sydney Olympics, describing itself as culturally diverse despite a race debate that has alarmed parts of Asia.
"There's no problem with diverse, 10 out of 10 for diversity, and culturally sophisticated -- 10 out of 10," Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer told Reuters.

Fischer had just launched the government's promotional campaign for new trade links ahead of the Sydney 2000 Olympics at the National Trade and Investment Outlook conference, which is aimed largely at potential Asian business partners.

A debate has raged in the Australian media and parliament in the months since independent conservative parliamentarian Pauline Hanson said in her September maiden speech that Australia was in danger of being overrun by Asians.
Her comments were widely supported on radio talk shows and in letters to newspaper editors, and opinion polls showed a majority of Australians agreed with her comments.

Asian media condemned Prime Minister John Howard's initial silence on the comments and he eventually made a parliamentary statement supporting Australia's non-discriminatory immigration policy and opposing racism.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer has said the furore, which has dominated the media for months, could damage Australia's reputation and trade links with its neighbours.

Fischer said Australia's cultural links with the region showed it was now cross-pollinating with Asia and that recent by-elections had shown the public had rejected Hanson's agenda for reduced immigration from Asia.
"In the sense that Australia now has ballet companies performing in Shanghai, we have symphony orchestras from Asia performing here in Australia, this cross-pollination is fantastic.
"The Hanson agenda has now been rejected in two by-elections," he said, referring to defeats suffered by pro-Hanson parties in votes to the national and state parliaments.

"The government, the party, the opposition and the people are as one in support of strong links with Asia based on mutual respect and are as one on a non-discriminatory approach to immigration policy," he said.
